rq: Research question / objective
Themes and subthemes
Answer in brief (with key evidence)
Primary RQ: How do older Syrian refugees in Jordan perceive the role of economic engagement in influencing psychosocial well-being?
T3 (all subthemes), T1.3, T2.1, T4.4

Participants saw economic engagement as central to well-being through four routes: dignity and independence (E2-266, E5-196, E9-065), relief from rumination and empty time (E1-243, E8-431–442), the ability to fulfil provider and host roles (E1-271, E4-232), and social regard (E3-143, E4-106). The relationship was conditional: insecure or degrading work brought new strain (E6-127, E7-601, E10-157), and two participants held that dignity itself does not depend on money (E3-296, E6-140).
SQ1: How does economic engagement (formal/informal) affect older Syrian refugees?

Engagement was mostly informal, short-term or home-based. It secured survival and some relief and purpose, but exposed participants to very low pay (E4-125, E10-097), wage theft (E5-101), exploitation without legal protection (E3-233–251), insult and extortion (E7-597–602) and sudden loss (E1-128, E8-258). Stable work (E6, E9) gave comfort and, for E9, decision-making power (E9-043), but not freedom from worry (E6-184–191). For women, entry into paid work was also a development (E1-079–081); for men, the family's reliance on others' earnings was experienced as loss (E4-100, E7-300).
SQ2: How do experiences of exclusion affect self-reported anxiety, depressive feelings, isolation and meaning?

Exclusion — by age ceilings, permits, nationality, wasta and lack of capital — was described as qahr, humiliation and being 'crushed' (E2-301, E4-205, E7-430), with insomnia (E2-096), withdrawal (E4-041–044), fear about tomorrow (E3-348) and family conflict (E8-431–496, E10-076). Meaning was sustained through faith, children and contributing to others (E7-611–628, E9-085), with E4 as the case in which these resources were not evident (E4-250–254). K6 results are descriptive only (Memo 3).
Objective 2: identity and dignity after forced displacement
Identity was anchored in past work and standing ('master of oneself'); displacement produced role reversal, gendered role change and humiliation (sections 7.1, 7.3).
Objective 3: income and psychological well-being, and feeling useful to the community
Income was linked to reassurance and relief (E10-162, E9-067); feeling useful came especially from teaching, guiding and helping (E7-628, E2-436, E1-160).
Objective 4: hope and imagined roles in rebuilding Syria

Hope was conditional: modest work-based aspirations and a belief that the generation can rebuild through experience, guidance and reconciliation 'if conditions are prepared' (E10-208–214), alongside doubts about capital and exhaustion (E8-610, E1-312).
Objective 5: suggestions for policymakers

Participants asked for projects and tools rather than cash, fair selection without wasta, removal of age ceilings in training, recognition of experience, and priority for widows, the sick and those unable to work (E3-495, E2-465–479, E4-384, E8-803–808, E9-085).
negative: Age is experienced as a barrier to work
Participants who denied age discrimination or said age is 'just a number'
Age-based exclusion is real in programme criteria but is not uniformly experienced in employment; participants resist ageist premises while some internalise decline (E3-396, E8-649–658).
Money and work are the basis of dignity
Dignity is intrinsic and does not depend on money
The threat to dignity lies in dependence, servility and conditional help rather than in poverty itself.
Even with income, insecurity keeps people anxious
Security and predictability of income matter more than income as such.
Where everyone is poor ('we are all refugees') or where family authority is protected, regard may not depend on money.
Women gaining roles; men keeping authority
Role change is gendered and not uniform.
The most isolated participant lacked the resources others relied on — relevant for practice and referral.
Older refugees want work and projects
Wish to rest and be secure
Rights-based support must include social protection, not only economic activation.
Training seen as useless or too late
Programmes must be relevant, linked to tools/capital and timely.
Reconstruction belongs to the young; no means; no respect for elders
Capacity is conditional on resources and on intergenerational respect.
